description.purpose: An interactive canvas served over HTTP under the render cell's own path. The picture is generated server-side by a code cell; the browser owns only the drag. The first thing it draws is the colony itself.
description.use_when: Somebody should see and rearrange something the colony knows, in a browser. One canvy per canvas: two canvases are two hives, told apart by their paths, which is what makes one nginx location block a complete access rule for one of them.
description.not_in_scope: It draws nothing its store does not hold. The topology snapshot arrives on a timer through this hive's OWN `./probe -> /colony/graph` lane (GH #163: the one absolute endpoint a mutation may draw, because it is the colony's read-only topology endpoint and the sanctioned alternative to reading `colony.db`), so the canvas is as fresh as that timer and as whoever else feeds its store. No realtime push: a viewer sees a change when it joins or interacts, not when another viewer moves a box. No object library beyond cells, hives and edges. No signed session token, which is only needed once a link has to survive being handed to a third party. And no interior address: `params.ports` is empty, so the render cell and the store are not endpoints -- a caller names the hive and a lane (in_refresh in, surface out).
examples: GET /surface/org/acme/member/alice/canvy/render -- the colony, draggable, arrangement persistent
socket event node:moved -> render -> store -> render -> the browser (two code cell calls, ~34 ms)
refresh (timer, 60s) -> probe -> /colony/graph -> probe -> store -- one snapshot row. The same snapshot on demand: an edge onto the HIVE path carrying hop.route == 'in_refresh'.
